evidence_quotes.quote: During dry seasons, the boreholes are always crowded, and due to that people spend several hours without getting water to fetch.

The study revealed that maintenance payments are not made on a regular basis. Rather, community members are required to contribute funds only when the borehole breaks down or shows signs of malfunction. These contributions are mobilized by the WSMTs to ensure timely repairs.

In these meetings, both male and female members of the WSMTs were allowed to participate and share their ideas and opinions on the best ways to govern the community’s boreholes. There were no restrictions on participation, ensuring that everyone had a voice.

Five communities (Ga, Dorimon, Zanko, Vieri, and Naaha) were selected based on accessibility, borehole presence, and active Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs). The study involved 37 community-level participants selected through purposive sampling.
However, in some communities such as Dorimon, Vieri and Ga, it is discovered that violators who repeatedly violate these regulations are restricted from fetching water for a specific period.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines community-level rural drinking-water service access via handpump boreholes across five rural communities in Wa West District, Ghana.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both readings of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines local water governance institutions (Water and Sanitation Management Teams, WSMTs), community operational regulations, and women's participation in rule-making. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, Research Question (a) and Section 5.1-5.3 directly examine concrete rule-type mechanisms governing drinking-water access: daily operating-hour/rationing rules (locking boreholes from 7:00-7:30 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. and upon early signs of malfunction), user and water-use restrictions (prohibiting children from pumping, prohibiting borehole water for brick molding, prohibiting cooking pots at water points), tariff/cost-recovery rules and ability-to-pay accommodation (event-driven repair contributions of GH₵ 1-7 for men and GH₵ 2 for women in certain communities, set by consensus according to household financial strength), and enforcement sanctions (GH₵ 100 fines, compulsory cleaning, and temporary exclusion of repeat violators from fetching water), alongside how gender-inclusive WSMT governance formulates and monitors these rules.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary empirical qualitative single-case study conducted in January-February 2025 across five rural communities in Wa West District using five focus group discussions with 37 purposively sampled WSMT members (18 men, 19 women), direct field observation with photographic documentation, and manual inductive thematic analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes relevant to drinking-water access, service availability, reliability/continuity, waiting time, affordability, and exclusion: frequent borehole breakdowns and functionality preservation, non-compliance with child-pumping bans observed in the field, dry-season crowding with multi-hour waits without getting water, restricted night-time/emergency service availability due to overnight locking, affordability of ad hoc repair levies, and temporary exclusion of repeat rule violators from fetching water.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and sample (37 WSMT members in 5 rural communities in Wa West District, Ghana; community/WSMT and household user levels), exposure (local borehole governance rules, fee/enforcement mechanisms, and gender-inclusive WSMT rule-making), outcomes (qualitative borehole functionality, hours of availability, waiting/crowding, exclusion of violators, and fee burden), and study design (qualitative single-case study with FGDs and observation) are clearly identified. Lacks quantitative effect estimates for meta-analysis, which is a synthesis gate rather than a review-inclusion gate per Criterion 6 and the qualitative socio-legal safeguard.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Qualitative single-case study using focus group discussions, direct field observations, and manual inductive thematic analysis
population_and_sample: Five rural communities (Ga, Dorimon, Zanko, Vieri, and Naaha) in Wa West District, Upper West Region, Ghana; 37 purposively sampled Water and Sanitation Management Team (WSMT) members (18 male, 19 female) across 5 focus group discussions, plus direct field observations of borehole use (units of analysis: community/WSMT and rural borehole users)
exposure: Community-level borehole operational, rationing, cost-recovery, and enforcement rules (overnight and preventive borehole locking, event-driven repair fee contributions, prohibitions on child pumping, construction water use, and metal cooking pots, monetary fines, and temporary bans on fetching water) and gender-inclusive rule formulation by Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs)
outcome: Qualitative drinking-water borehole functionality and reliability, hours of service availability under overnight locking, dry-season crowding and waiting times, affordability of ad hoc repair contributions, rule compliance, and temporary exclusion of repeat violators from fetching water
rationale: This primary qualitative empirical study in rural Ghana meets all review inclusion criteria (c1-c6). It examines rural community drinking-water access via handpump boreholes (c1) and directly investigates rule-type governance mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 — including WSMT rule formulation, overnight locking/rationing rules, event-driven maintenance fee rules and ability-to-pay discretion, use/user eligibility restrictions, and enforcement sanctions including fines and temporary exclusion from fetching water (c2). It uses primary focus group discussions (n = 37 across 5 communities) and direct field observations (c3), reports qualitative outcomes on service availability, borehole reliability/breakdowns, crowding, fee affordability, and user exclusion (c4), and clearly specifies population, exposure, outcome, and design in English (c5, c6). Per the protocol safeguard on qualitative socio-legal studies, lack of a quantitative effect estimate precludes meta-analysis pooling but not systematic-review inclusion for mechanism synthesis.
